concept.name: Lock-Free Atomics

relationships.description: Connects Lock-Free Atomics to python concurrency nogil in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Lock-free atomics coordinate shared state across threads using hardware compare-and-swap (CAS) primitives and explicit memory orderings so at least one thread always makes progress without OS mutex blocking.
spark.keyTakeaway: Lock-free atomics eliminate mutex context switches and deadlocks, but high contention still causes CPU cache-line bouncing and subtle ABA/memory-ordering bugs.

concept.whyItMatters: When dozens of cores contend on a single mutex, OS scheduling, priority inversion, and lock convoys cap throughput long before CPU cores are saturated. Hardware atomic instructions (`CMPXCHG`, `LDXR/STXR`) and carefully chosen memory barriers let high-throughput queues, ring buffers, and counters scale with bounded tail latency.
whenToUse: High-frequency counters, metrics, flags, and sequence generators where a single atomic instruction (`fetch_add`, `LongAdder`) replaces a mutex.
Wait-free/lock-free SPSC or MPMC ring buffers (e.g., LMAX Disruptor, audio/telemetry pipelines) where kernel context switches break microsecond latency budgets.
Read-mostly shared metadata swapped atomically via immutable snapshots or RCU (Read-Copy-Update) pointers.
whenNotToUse: Multi-object invariants or complex transactional state machines where fine-grained `Mutex`/`RwLock` is simpler, easier to prove correct, and fast enough.
I/O-bound code paths (database calls, network sockets) where microsecond lock savings are invisible compared to millisecond I/O.
Write-heavy shared single variables across 64+ cores without striping or sharding, where cache-line bouncing makes naive CAS slower than a well-partitioned lock.
keyPoints: Lock-free guarantees system-wide progress (some thread finishes in finite steps); wait-free guarantees per-thread progress; obstruction-free only guarantees progress in isolation.
Modern CPUs implement atomics via `CMPXCHG` (x86-64) or Load-Linked/Store-Conditional (`LDXR`/`STXR` on ARM64) backed by the MESI/MOESI cache coherence protocol.
Memory orderings (`relaxed`, `acquire`, `release`, `seq_cst`) control compiler and CPU instruction reordering—overusing `seq_cst` adds unnecessary `MFENCE`/`DMB` barriers on ARM/POWER.
Lock-free linked structures face the ABA problem (a pointer changes A → B → A between read and CAS) and unsafe memory reclamation while other threads still hold references.
False sharing—two unrelated atomics sitting on the same 64-byte L1 cache line—destroys scalability and is fixed with padding (`alignas(64)` or `@Contended`).

examples.title: Eliminating Counter Contention with Striped Atomics
examples.scenario: A 64-core API gateway increments a single global `AtomicLong` request counter on every packet, causing p99 latency to degrade under cache-line bouncing.
examples.outcome: Switching to `LongAdder` (striped per-thread cells padded to 64-byte cache lines) cut atomic update cost from ~380 ns to ~8 ns and restored linear core scaling.

examples.title: Lock-Free Config Hot-Reload via Acquire-Release
examples.scenario: Routing workers read a 50,000-rule routing table on every request while a background thread refreshes rules every 10 seconds.
examples.outcome: Publishing an immutable snapshot pointer with `memory_order_release` and reading with `memory_order_acquire` achieved zero-lock reads with < 5 ns overhead.

tradeOffs.pro: Eliminates OS scheduler preemption delays, deadlocks, and priority inversion on critical paths.
tradeOffs.con: Proving correctness across weak memory models (ARM64) and safe reclamation (EBR/hazard pointers) is orders of magnitude harder than mutexes.

tradeOffs.factor: CAS Retry Loops vs. Contended Mutexes
tradeOffs.pro: Under low-to-moderate contention, uncontended CAS takes 5–15 ns with zero kernel syscalls.
tradeOffs.con: Under extreme write contention on one cache line, CAS spin retries burn 100% CPU and starve threads.

tradeOffs.pro: `relaxed` and `acquire/release` avoid full store-load fences (`MFENCE`/`DMB ISH`), boosting ARM64 throughput.
tradeOffs.con: A single misplaced `relaxed` load can cause data races that only manifest under rare CPU store-buffer reorderings in production.

failureModes.name: The ABA Problem
failureModes.description: Thread 1 reads node `A`, gets preempted, Thread 2 pops `A`, pushes `B`, and re-pushes `A` at the same address; Thread 1's CAS succeeds and corrupts the freelist.
failureModes.mitigation: Pack a monotonically increasing version tag with the pointer (128-bit `CMPXCHG16B` / `AtomicStampedReference`) or use Epoch-Based Reclamation.

failureModes.name: Use-After-Free During Reclamation
failureModes.description: A thread frees a popped node while another concurrent reader is still dereferencing its `next` pointer.
failureModes.mitigation: Defer freeing via Hazard Pointers, Epoch-Based Reclamation (crossbeam-epoch), or garbage-collected runtimes.

failureModes.name: False Sharing on 64-Byte Cache Lines
failureModes.description: Independent atomic counters for different threads sit in the same 64-byte cache line, forcing constant MESI invalidations across cores.
failureModes.mitigation: Pad hot atomics to cache-line boundaries (`alignas(64)` in C++/Rust, `@Contended` in Java with `-XX:-RestrictContended`).

failureModes.name: Weak Memory Model Reordering
failureModes.description: Code tested on x86-64 (strong TSO memory model) silently breaks on ARM64 Graviton/Apple Silicon due to relaxed load/store reordering.
failureModes.mitigation: Use explicit `acquire`/`release` pairs for publication, test on ARM64 hardware, and run ThreadSanitizer (TSan) or Loom/CDSChecker.

commonMistakes: Assuming `volatile` in C/C++ provides atomicity or thread synchronization (it only prevents compiler caching for MMIO).
Using `compare_exchange_weak` without a retry loop (spurious LL/SC failures on ARM64 will drop updates).
Checking two separate atomic variables sequentially and expecting the pair to be mutually consistent.
Building a custom lock-free MPMC queue in production instead of using battle-tested libraries (`crossbeam`, `folly::MPMCQueue`, `Disruptor`).
Ignoring memory reclamation and leaking nodes or calling `free()` immediately after CAS.

sections.content:
## The idea

Lock-free programming replaces mutual exclusion (where one thread sleeps while another holds a lock) with optimistic **Read-Modify-Write (RMW)** loops backed by CPU hardware:

- **Compare-And-Swap (CAS)**: Atomically compares a memory word against an expected value and swaps in a new value only if they match, returning whether it succeeded.
- **Progress Guarantees**: *Wait-free* means every thread completes in a bounded number of steps (e.g., `fetch_add`); *Lock-free* means at least one thread always makes progress even if others are preempted mid-operation.
- **Coherence & Ordering**: Hardware cache coherence (MESI/MOESI) serializes writes to each 64-byte cache line, while memory orderings (`relaxed`, `acquire`, `release`, `seq_cst`) tell both the compiler and CPU store buffers which reorderings are forbidden.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a lock-free Treiber stack `push(node)` and `pop()` using tagged pointers to prevent ABA:

1. **Prepare**: Thread T1 allocates `new_node`, writes `new_node.data = 42`, and loads `old_head = head.load(acquire)` (containing pointer `P1` and version tag `v=7`).
2. **Link Speculatively**: T1 sets `new_node.next = P1` locally—no other thread can see `new_node` yet.
3. **Atomic Publish**: T1 executes `head.compare_exchange_weak(old_head, {new_node, v=8}, release, relaxed)`.
4. **Contention Handling**: If T2 updated `head` to `{P2, v=8}` in the meantime, T1's CAS fails, reloads `{P2, v=8}` into `old_head`, updates `new_node.next = P2`, and retries.
5. **Safe Pop**: When T2 pops, it reads `old_head`, enters an epoch/hazard guard so `old_head` cannot be freed, CAS-swaps `head` to `{old_head.next, v+1}`, and retires `old_head` to the epoch reclaimer.

nodes.sublabel: Deferred free list after grace period

edges.label: RFO (Read For Ownership)
edges.title: Claim exclusive cache-line ownership
edges.description: Core 0 requests Exclusive/Modified state for the 64-byte line holding the atomic head pointer.

edges.label: Invalidate line
edges.title: Invalidate stale peer copies
edges.description: Coherence fabric invalidates Core 1's shared copy so the CAS executes atomically.

edges.label: CAS(old, {new, v+1})
edges.title: Execute release-ordered CAS
edges.description: Core 0 publishes new_node with incremented version tag; retries if old_head changed.

edges.label: Acquire load
edges.title: Fetch updated cache line
edges.description: Core 1 incurs a cache miss, fetches the Modified line, and sees all writes prior to release.

edges.label: Retire old node
edges.title: Defer memory reclamation
edges.description: After popping via tagged CAS, Core 1 places the removed node in an epoch retire queue.

edges.label: Reclaim after grace period
edges.title: Free unreferenced nodes safely
edges.description: Once all active threads advance past the old epoch, memory is safely returned to the allocator.

data.caption: Lock-free correctness requires pairing tagged CAS and acquire/release fences with safe memory reclamation and cache-line awareness.

sections.content:
## Memory orderings & hardware models

Compilers and CPUs aggressively reorder independent loads and stores to hide memory latency (~60–100 ns to DRAM). Memory orderings constrain that reordering:

- **`relaxed`**: Guarantees atomicity and modification order of that single variable only—ideal for telemetry counters.
- **`acquire` / `release`**: Forms a *happens-before* edge between a releasing store in Thread A and an acquiring load in Thread B that observes it. On x86-64 (TSO), plain `MOV` already provides acquire/release; on ARM64, it compiles to `LDAR` / `STLR`.
- **`seq_cst`**: Enforces a single total global order across all threads, emitting a heavy `MFENCE` / `LOCK XCHG` on x86-64 or `DMB ISH` on ARM64 for store-load ordering.

## Comparing synchronization mechanisms

| Mechanism | Uncontended Latency | High-Contention Behavior | Progress Guarantee | Memory Reclamation Needed? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **OS Mutex (`pthread_mutex` / `ReentrantLock`)** | ~15–25 ns (futex fast path) | Kernel sleep + context switch (~2–10 µs) | Blocking (deadlock/inversion risk) | No (protected by lock) |
| **Single `AtomicLong` CAS** | ~5–15 ns | Severe cache-line bouncing (~300–800 ns) | Lock-free | No (value type) |
| **Striped `LongAdder` / Sharded Counter** | ~5–10 ns | Scales linearly across cores (~8–15 ns) | Wait-free (per-cell) | No |
| **Tagged-CAS Linked Structure + EBR** | ~15–30 ns | Retry spin under burst | Lock-free | Yes (EBR / Hazard Pointers) |
| **SPSC Ring Buffer (`acquire`/`release`)** | ~3–8 ns | Zero CAS needed; bounded wait | Wait-free | No (preallocated array) |

## Failure modes

1. **Cache-Line Ping-Ponging**: 32+ threads performing `CAS` on one shared head pointer saturate the CPU interconnect with Read-For-Ownership (RFO) traffic, dropping throughput below a mutex. *Mitigation*: Use bounded backoff, combining funnels, or sharded/SPSC queues.
2. **ARM64 vs. x86-64 Heisenbugs**: Missing `acquire`/`release` barriers often pass 100% of tests on x86-64 (strong TSO) and corrupt pointers in production on ARM64 Graviton. *Mitigation*: Test under ThreadSanitizer, Loom (Rust), or GenMC.
3. **ABA Pointer Reuse**: Allocators (`jemalloc`, `tcmalloc`) aggressively reuse recently freed addresses in thread-local caches, making ABA collisions frequent under load. *Mitigation*: Pair 128-bit double-width CAS with monotonic version tags or Epoch-Based Reclamation.
4. **Livelock Under `compare_exchange_weak`**: Spurious LL/SC failures on ARM64 or constant peer interference can stall progress if loops lack exponential pause (`_mm_pause` / `yield`). *Mitigation*: Insert `CPU_PAUSE` hints in retry loops and cap spin counts before backing off.

## Production patterns & alternatives

In practice, elite systems avoid general lock-free linked lists in favor of three high-leverage patterns:

- **Single-Producer Single-Consumer (SPSC) Ring Buffers**: Require only `acquire`/`release` on `head` and `tail` indices—no CAS, no ABA, and cache-line-padded indices.
- **Striped / Sharded Counters (`LongAdder`)**: Partition updates by thread/core ID into 64-byte padded slots and sum only on read.
- **RCU / Immutable Snapshot Swaps**: Writers build a new immutable config/index off-path, swap one atomic pointer with `release`, and reclaim the old version after a grace period.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Benchmark against a fine-grained mutex or `LongAdder` first to confirm lock contention is actually the bottleneck.
- [ ] Pad hot atomic fields to 64-byte cache-line boundaries (`alignas(64)` / `@Contended`) to prevent false sharing.
- [ ] Specify explicit memory orderings (`acquire`/`release` for publication, `relaxed` for independent counters) and document the happens-before invariant.
- [ ] Solve ABA and safe memory reclamation explicitly (tagged pointers, Hazard Pointers, or EBR) for any dynamic node structure.
- [ ] Verify under ThreadSanitizer / Loom and stress-test on weak-memory-model hardware (ARM64).

interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Lock-Free Atomics. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?

nodes.label: Epoch Reclaimer
nodes.role: Deferred free list after grace period

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Lock-free atomics coordinate shared state across threads using hardware compare-and-swap (CAS) primitives and explicit memory orderings so at least one thread always makes progress without OS mutex blocking.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: MESI Coherence Fabric applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Epoch Reclaimer.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Epoch Reclaimer experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Pack a monotonically increasing version tag with the pointer (128-bit `CMPXCHG16B` / `AtomicStampedReference`) or use Epoch-Based Reclamation.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Lock-free atomics eliminate mutex context switches and deadlocks, but high contention still causes CPU cache-line bouncing and subtle ABA/memory-ordering bugs.
Avoid trap: Assuming `volatile` in C/C++ provides atomicity or thread synchronization (it only prevents compiler caching for MMIO).
Avoid trap: Using `compare_exchange_weak` without a retry loop (spurious LL/SC failures on ARM64 will drop updates).
When to reach for it: High-frequency counters, metrics, flags, and sequence generators where a single atomic instruction (`fetch_add`, `LongAdder`) replaces a mutex.
When to reach for it: Wait-free/lock-free SPSC or MPMC ring buffers (e.g., LMAX Disruptor, audio/telemetry pipelines) where kernel context switches break microsecond latency budgets.

putItTogether.title: Putting Lock Free Atomics Together
putItTogether.summary: Lock-free atomics eliminate mutex context switches and deadlocks, but high contention still causes CPU cache-line bouncing and subtle ABA/memory-ordering bugs.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Lock Free Atomics before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Switching to `LongAdder` (striped per-thread cells padded to 64-byte cache lines) cut atomic update cost from ~380 ns to ~8 ns and restored linear core scaling.
